title: Currencies and Foreign Exchange
intro: The foreign exchange (FX) market is the largest market in the world: about \$9.6 trillion a day changed hands in the Bank for International Settlements' 2025 survey, more than the yearly output of most countries. Even if you never trade a currency, you hold currency risk the moment you own a foreign stock or bond. This page covers how exchange rates are quoted, who trades them, and what moves them.

blocks.text: A currency pair is written BASE/QUOTE and its price is how many units of the quote currency buy one unit of the base. EUR/USD = 1.0850 means one euro costs \$1.085. USD/JPY = 150.00 means one dollar costs 150 yen. If EUR/USD rises, the euro has strengthened (or the dollar weakened).

items: Market conventions put the euro first in almost every pair, then the pound, the Australian and New Zealand dollars, then the US dollar. So it's EUR/USD, GBP/USD, AUD/USD, but USD/JPY, USD/CHF, USD/CAD.

The majors are the most traded pairs against the dollar: EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD, NZD/USD. Crosses don't include the dollar (EUR/JPY, EUR/GBP, AUD/JPY). Nicknames: 'cable' (GBP/USD, after the transatlantic telegraph cable), 'fiber' (EUR/USD), 'loonie' (CAD), 'kiwi' (NZD), 'swissie' (CHF).
A pip is the fourth decimal (0.0001) in most pairs and the second (0.01) in yen pairs. A move in EUR/USD from 1.0850 to 1.0875 is 25 pips.
A cross rate comes from two dollar rates: if EUR/USD = 1.08 and USD/JPY = 150, then EUR/JPY = $1.08 \times 150 = 162$.

blocks.text: Spot trades settle in two business days (one for USD/CAD). Forwards fix a rate for a later date; FX swaps combine a spot and an opposite forward and are the biggest single part of the market, used by banks and companies to fund themselves in another currency. Retail traders usually use spot contracts with a broker that rolls positions overnight, paying or receiving the interest-rate difference.

items: Companies paying for imports, receiving export revenue, or hedging foreign profits.
Investors buying foreign stocks and bonds, and deciding whether to hedge the currency.
Banks and dealers making markets; the largest trading centers are London, New York, Singapore, Hong Kong and Tokyo.

Central banks managing reserves and sometimes intervening to weaken or support their currency (Japan sold dollars to support the yen in 2022 and 2024; Switzerland bought euros for years to weaken the franc).
Speculators and hedge funds trading carry, trends and macro views.

Interest rates: higher rates (relative to other countries) attract capital and usually strengthen a currency, at least in the short run. Expected changes in central bank policy are the biggest single driver of major pairs.
Inflation: over long periods, high-inflation currencies lose value against low-inflation ones (purchasing power parity).
Growth and trade: a current account surplus means a country earns more foreign currency than it spends; commodity exporters move with their exports' prices.
Risk appetite: in a crisis money flows to safe havens (the dollar, yen, Swiss franc) and out of higher-yielding and emerging currencies.
Politics, policy and capital controls: elections, sanctions, fiscal crises and controls on moving money.

blocks.text: Exchange rates are notoriously hard to forecast. Meese and Rogoff (1983) showed that standard economic models could not beat a simple random walk at horizons up to a year, and the result has largely held up. Long-run valuation (PPP) and interest-rate differentials have some value; short-run forecasting is close to a coin toss.
Your return on a foreign asset in your home currency is approximately the asset's local return plus the change in the foreign currency's value:

blocks.tex: 1 + R_{home} = (1 + R_{local})(1 + R_{fx}) \;\Rightarrow\; R_{home} \approx R_{local} + R_{fx}

blocks.text: A US investor whose European stocks gained 10% in euros while the euro fell 8% made only about 1.2%. Over decades currency moves have tended to wash out for stocks, but over a few years they can add or subtract a lot; for foreign bonds they can make up most of the risk. The next two pages cover the main currencies and the models (parity, carry, hedging).

blocks.title: Cross rate
blocks.text: GBP/USD is 1.27 and USD/JPY is 152. What is GBP/JPY?
solution: One pound buys \$1.27, and each dollar buys 152 yen: $1.27 \times 152 = 193.04$ yen per pound.

blocks.title: Foreign return
blocks.text: A US investor buys Japanese stocks. Over a year they rise 15% in yen, while USD/JPY goes from 140 to 155. What was the return in dollars?
solution: The yen weakened: each yen is worth $1/155$ dollars instead of $1/140$, a change of $140/155 - 1 \approx -9.7\%$.
Dollar return $= 1.15 \times 0.903 - 1 \approx +3.9\%$. Note that USD/JPY rising means the yen fell.
